strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching failure: seam cutting cannot conceal every residual misalignment. Repairing problematic patches with dense correspondence, then reconnecting local seams through fixed boundary labels, is a coherent and potentially useful approach.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets. Figures 1, 7, 10, and 11 show credible improvements to curbs, stairs, and other structures. The 20-participant user study provides supporting perceptual evidence, with the proposed method receiving 108 of 160 first-place votes.
The runtime comparisons use the same hardware and indicate a useful computational advantage over iterative seam estimation [17] on expensive cases, for the evaluated processing stage.
The pipeline is generally understandable, reused methods and public datasets are cited, and the explicit failure example usefully identifies the method's dependence on the initial alignment.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution is insufficiently isolated. SSIM-based seam evaluation comes from [17], seam-guided alignment is already represented by SEAGULL [18], and dense matching uses SIFT flow. The distinctive contribution is their localized integration and flow modification, but no dataset-wide ablations establish the benefits of quality-guided patch selection or sigmoid weighting. Figure 4 provides only a single illustrative comparison.

Quantitative comparisons are restricted to two seam-cutting methods [16,17]. The closest seam-driven alternatives [18,26] receive only limited qualitative comparison, while relevant parallax-aware methods already cited, such as [9,12], are not evaluated. The evidence therefore establishes improvement over the selected seam cutters more convincingly than competitiveness for large-parallax stitching.

Perceptual validation remains limited. Equation (5) uses essentially the same SSIM criterion that guides repair, measuring local seam consistency without adequately assessing overall geometric distortion or content preservation. The independent user study helps, but its eight examples were manually selected as controversial; selection criteria, presentation randomization, and per-scene results or uncertainty are not reported.

The central flow modification is underspecified. Section 3.4 writes the modified displacement as f(V), but Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized spatial position. The actual vector transformation and its handling of different seam orientations are not explicitly defined. Patch construction, overlapping-patch handling, and SIFT-flow settings also need clarification for reproducibility.

The claim of almost removing the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 still assumes small residual displacement within extracted patches. Moreover, the plausibility test max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) in Section 3.3 can accept a uniformly high-error seam, so it does not reliably distinguish good alignment from widespread failure. The acknowledged limitations support a narrower claim of repairing localized residual errors.

There are correctable reporting inconsistencies: Figures 6, 8, and 9 use baseline reference numbers inconsistent with the text, and Table 1 gives 159 rankings for [17] and 161 for [16], although the described protocol implies 160 per method. These should be corrected, but the principal reasons for weak rejection are the missing comparative evidence, ablations, and methodological specification.
